body: I didn't test, but possibly related to #105746? CC @mihe

> I didn't test, but possibly related to [#105746](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105746)?

Given that adding a `physics_system->OptimizeBroadPhase()` call to `JoltSpace3D::flush_pending_objects` "fixes" the problem, it's almost certainly a regression from #107454.

Would you mind further explaining your real world use-case for this particular setup @jon1solution? The MRP here pretty much showcases the worst-case scenario with the current approach, where you're ray-casting after every single added body, within a `@tool` script in particular, thus completely nullifying the batching that replaced the above mentioned `OptimizeBroadPhase` call in #107454, resulting in some very unfortunate spatial partitioning.

If you're just profiling for the sake of profiling then I would prefer that we leave this as-is.

Also, it's probably important to note that these numbers only apply when done within the editor viewport through a `@tool` script and not during normal game runtime, as stepping the physics simulation (which doesn't happen in the editor viewport) would perform the above mentioned optimization.

Ah, I did not explain my use case well.  Please note that this isn't just a performance bug...if you let this MRP continue to run in v.5-beta1 the editor will eventually crash.  There are actually 2 different things going on in this MRP: 

1. I am adding a single raycast after adding a body as a workaround for [Issue # 107366](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/107366).  That workaround is no longer needed in the v4.5-beta1, but this code would still crash when you tested it in the 4.5-dev5, so I left it in.  I am not profiling this raycast, it is strictly a work-around.
2. After adding geometry, in this MRP, I an doing a bunch of raycasts as a stand-in for the raycasts my game is using when checking for bullet hits.  These are the raycasts I was profiling to try to optimize the projectile code, when I noticed this issue.

In the game, I am generating interior building geometry procedurally as the user gets close to the exterior of the building, then removing interior geometry when it's no longer needed.  That drives the removal of old geometry, and the regular creation of new geometry.

We are also doing some minimal projectile physics (drag, wind, gravity) for each of the bullets, with a target limit of 2048 projectiles active.  This means I end up running as many as 2048 raycasts for each physics process.

The non-minimal test project looks like this:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b98caf41-2373-48ce-a0c5-9896782882b3)

Just a note: in v4.5-beta1 the average raycast execution time seems to climb pretty linearly with the total number of collision objects that have ever been added.  In v4.5-dev5 the time seems linear with the current number of active collision objects.

Is it possible that in v4.5-beta1 the old collision geometry is not being removed when I call queue_free() on the parent Node3D?

> I am adding a single raycast after adding a body as a workaround for #107366. That workaround is no longer needed in the v4.5-beta1

Right. That workaround becomes very detrimental after #107454, meaning 4.5-beta1.

> but this code would still crash when you tested it in the 4.5-dev5, so I left it in

I'm able to reproduce the crash even after removing that `test_raycast()` call in `AdderState.ADDING`, in 4.5-beta1 (or latest `master` rather).

The crash seems to be about Jolt running out of available nodes inside of its `QuadTree`, so I'm guessing you're running into a variation of the scenario that was talked about [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/107454#issuecomment-2970289142), but I'm not sure if the circumstances here are applicable to that scenario.

> After adding geometry, in this MRP, I am doing a bunch of raycasts as a stand-in for the raycasts my game is using when checking for bullet hits.
> [...]
> In the game, I am generating interior building geometry procedurally as the user gets close to the exterior of the building, then removing interior geometry when it's no longer needed. That drives the removal of old geometry, and the regular creation of new geometry.

I take it you mean during actual game runtime then, meaning this isn't something that actually needs to be done in a `@tool` context?

> Just a note: in v4.5-beta1 the average raycast execution time seems to climb pretty linearly with the total number of collision objects that have ever been added. In v4.5-dev5 the time seems linear with the current number of active collision objects.
>
> Is it possible that in v4.5-beta1 the old collision geometry is not being removed when I call queue_free() on the parent Node3D?

It doesn't have anything to do with collision geometry per se. It's the spatial partitioning (quadtree) within Jolt itself that never goes through its (potentially costly) cleanup/optimization like it did prior to #107454, where it happened when ray-casting after having added at least 128 bodies since the last ray-cast.

---

@jrouwe I'd be curious to hear your thoughts on this.

Using pseudocode similar to your own, is it expected to run out of nodes in a scenario like this?:

```
loop forever
    bodies = {}
    do 1500 times
        bodies.push_back(create_body)
    add_bodies(bodies) // due to intersect_ray
    for body in bodies
        destroy_body(body)
```

When writing it out like this it does seem very similar to what you talked about [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/107454#issuecomment-2970289142), so I'm guessing it is expected?

Sorry, I have just been profiling things inside the editor for ease of testing.  

You are correct, running the MRP does not crash, and the raycast timing remains consistent...it is only running it as a tool script in the editor that crashes.

Of course, I would still like to continue testing my code inside the editor...is there some kind of workaround where I can trigger the quadtree update internally based on Engine.is_editor_hint()?

> Of course, I would still like to continue testing my code inside the editor...is there some kind of workaround where I can trigger the quadtree update internally based on Engine.is_editor_hint()?

Not really, no.

The only decent solution to this that I can see (from the Godot side of things) would be for us to get even more creative about when/where to call `JPH::PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase`, like maybe scheduling some arbitrary timer whenever pending bodies are flushed and bumping that timer if more bodies come in, or something along those lines.

However, I fear that would just lead to other weird quirks with random editor stutters (for large enough scenes) that can't easily be traced back to the physics side of things.

Given how esoteric the presented use-case is, I'm not sure it's really worth addressing this at all.

My main concern now is if this can somehow happen during just normal editor use as well, where you maybe add a bunch of physics bodies through the Scene dock like normal, then maybe do some "Snap Object to Floor", then remove some bodies, then add some bodies, do some more "Snap Object to Floor", etc. etc. until you crash.

I'm guessing/hoping you would need to do that _a lot_ (and in a very specific sequence) to actually trigger this crash though.

> Using pseudocode similar to your own, is it expected to run out of nodes in a scenario like this?

Yes, this is a scenario where you can run out of nodes as you use a lot of nodes to create a new section of the tree and then empty those nodes again when destroying objects. The nodes are not actually deleted until the world is stepped (delta time = 0 is ok) or optimize broad phase is called.

Does this really have to work with time being paused?

A work around could be to increase the max number of bodies (this also increases the number of nodes), but that will postpone and not fix running out.

An alternative could be for me to expose a function to query if the tree still has space so you could call OptimizeBroadPhase when running out.

> Does this really have to work with time being paused?

That's the question I guess. The use-case here isn't really something that I would normally expect to see in a `@tool` script (which are scripts that run in the editor viewport) at least with regards to removing large swathes of bodies over and over, which is a big part of the problem here I guess.

> until the world is stepped (delta time = 0 is ok)

Is there any functional difference between doing a step of 0 and calling `OptimizeBroadPhase`? ~~At a glance they seem to be doing largely the same thing.~~

EDIT: I see now that `OptimizeBroadPhase` does a full rebuild, whereas a step of 0 does not.

Either way, I would prefer not to ignore the `!active` state of the physics server if possible, especially not if it adds some non-trivial amount of overhead to the editor ticks.

> A work around could be to increase the max number of bodies (this also increases the number of nodes), but that will postpone and not fix running out.

Yeah, that wouldn't really fix this I guess.

> An alternative could be for me to expose a function to query if the tree still has space so you could call OptimizeBroadPhase when running out.

That sounds like an interesting option. That would at least resolve the crash in the rare circumstances that somebody runs into it.

I'm taking the liberty of reframing this issue to be about the crash instead, since that seems to be the more important aspect here. It still seems like a fairly niche/contrived scenario to me though, so I've dropped the severity on the release blocker as well.

Thank you for fixing the issue description!  I definitely agree that the scenario is niche, so a lower severity makes sense.  I wouldn't say contrived, though, as I ran into the issue while doing actual development on some procedural generation code.  I noticed the slowdown first, but eventually the editor would crash, and now I realize those were related.

It just occurred to me, I wonder if just changing properties of CSG elements is handled internally as removing the old collision bodies then adding in new ones?  I'll try to test that.

EDIT - Just updating the already existing CSG elements does not show the problem.  I changed each CSGCombiner3D to have 2 offset CSGBox3D's, then instead of removing and recreating the elements I simply changed their sizes.  There was the expected pause each time the geometry was updated, but the raycast timing stayed consistent and the editor still hasn't crashed.

Oh, I just found a workaround!

I can simply enable the physics engine using `PhysicsServer3D.set_active()` while adding the new geometry.

> I wouldn't say contrived, though, as I ran into the issue while doing actual development on some procedural generation code.

Fair enough. I was mostly thinking of testing/profiling runtime stuff within a `@tool` context, but I suppose it's not completely unthinkable for someone to be doing this kind of add->query->remove->repeat sequence as part of a procedural generation script that's only meant to run in a `@tool` context.

> I wonder if just changing properties of CSG elements is handled internally as removing the old collision bodies then adding in new ones?

It doesn't remove the whole body, no. It just does `set_faces(...)` on the underlying `ConcavePolygonShape3D`, which will just widen the Jolt quadtree node if needed, so there's no re-adding happening.

> I can simply enable the physics engine using `PhysicsServer3D.set_active()` while adding the new geometry.

I imagine that'll also start simulating any `RigidBody3D` you have in your scene though, but if you don't have any then that might work as a quick hack.

One thing that just hit me is that we don't actually need to imagine all of this happening within the context of a `@tool` script at all.

The simple act of switching scenes in the editor will remove all (except one) of the objects from the physics space used by the editor viewport, which will then be re-added once we open that scene again, while reusing that same physics space. So given sufficiently complex scenes you can end up removing and adding thousands of physics bodies as you switch between scenes.

This on its own isn't enough to cause any problems though, since you also need a physics query to prompt the pending bodies to actually be flushed, but seeing as how the "Snap Object to Floor" feature in the editor uses `intersect_ray`, it's not hard to imagine someone jumping between a bunch of different scenes and snapping objects down in each of them, creating largely the same scenario as the MRP here (without `add_raycast` enabled).

What's really strange though is that even if I call `JPH::PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase` as part of `JoltSpace3D::remove_object`, when we're down to this one persistent object (i.e. when the scene is closed or emptied out), I still end up with `intersect_ray` costing more and more over time, which would seem to suggest that Jolt's quadtree isn't in fact being cleaned up.

> I imagine that'll also start simulating any `RigidBody3D` you have in your scene though, but if you don't have any then that might work as a quick hack.

Good point, though I am actually shutting it back off in the next frame, so it only advanced a bit.  (I am guessing it would be a horrible idea to set `Engine.physics_ticks_per_second` to a really high number for that frame, then fixing it the next frame?)

> I am guessing it would be a horrible idea to set `Engine.physics_ticks_per_second` to a really high number for that frame, then fixing it the next frame?

You mean in order to get a smaller timestep? I'm not sure what that would fix exactly. If you want a time step of 0 then `Engine.time_scale` is your best option, but in a `@tool` context that'll presumably mess with the entire editor processing.

> What's really strange though is that even if I call `JPH::PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase` as part of `JoltSpace3D::remove_object`, when we're down to this one persistent object (i.e. when the scene is closed or emptied out), I still end up with `intersect_ray` costing more and more over time, which would seem to suggest that Jolt's quadtree isn't in fact being cleaned up.

@jrouwe, I don't fully understand why, but it seems this is because of this check:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9a3976097f5ac99ab3302193d40a944887206e95/thirdparty/jolt_physics/Jolt/Physics/Collision/BroadPhase/BroadPhaseQuadTree.cpp#L83

Since the one remaining/persistent object is an `Area3D`, only its broadphase layer (`AREA_UNDETECTABLE`) ends up actually passing this check and going through with the optimization/cleanup, whereas the rest of the (empty) layers (e.g. `BODY_STATIC`) are left as-is.

I'm not sure if this hack of mine is worth going through with, so don't feel too pressured to address this, but it does seem a little bit odd not to allow empty broadphase layers to be cleaned up during `OptimizeBroadPhase`, if it's actually intentional that is.

> One thing that just hit me is that we don't actually need to imagine all of this happening within the context of a `@tool` script at all.

Just to confirm that this crash does indeed happen when switching scenes as well, I threw together another MRP that uses a GDScript addon to open and close the main scene a bunch of times, and it does indeed crash the editor after 90-ish scene opens with this particular scene: [jolt-scene-switch-crash.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20946444/jolt-scene-switch-crash.zip) (photosensitivity warning, rapid flickering)

I wasn't sure how to programmatically invoke "Snap Object to Floor", so I simulated that with a single `intersect_ray` in a `@tool` script.

> @jrouwe, I don't fully understand why, but it seems this is because of this check:

That check is wrong indeed. It means that trees that have no bodies left will never get optimized. But a tree without bodies can still contain nodes, so by skipping this tree we're accumulating nodes and eventually running out of them.

I've created a fix for the issue. I haven't had time to verify that it actually fixes this MRP, but I could reproduce it in the unit test that I added to Jolt (and it's fixed now).

> I've created a fix for the issue.

Wonderful, thank you!

> I haven't had time to verify that it actually fixes this MRP

It wouldn't, since we don't currently call `OptimizeBroadPhase` anywhere, but I can confirm that it fixes the crash (and performance degradation) of my latest MRP, if you add this to the bottom of `JoltSpace3D::remove_object`:

```cpp
if (physics_system->GetNumBodies() <= 1) {
    physics_system->OptimizeBroadPhase();
}
```

It does also technically resolve the crash and performance degradation of the original MRP, but only because that script empties out the scene completely during its removal phase, which is hardly a given.

The discussions here have been a bit all over the place, but just to lay down my thought process more clearly, here's the situation as I see it:

- Something as common as switching scenes, with some "Snap Object to Floor" interspersed, will cause the editor to crash eventually, due to running out of nodes, which is not good.
- Adding something like your proposed ability to query the broadphase for available nodes would presumably resolve this crash entirely, for all possible scenarios, since we can then run `OptimizeBroadPhase` in `JoltSpace3D::flush_pending_objects` only when absolutely necessary, in order to make nodes available.
- This would not however solve the performance degradation of physics queries that would happen as you either switch scenes with some "Snap Object to Floor" interspersed, like what can be seen in my latest MRP, or when you procedurally generate (combined with queries and removals of) physics bodies from within a `@tool` script, like what can be seen in the original MRP.
- I'm not personally too bothered by this performance degradation. Nobody is going to complain that "Snap Object to Floor" is taking 200 μs instead of 50 μs (unless there are scenarios where this degradation becomes much worse?) nor do I see a major problem with queries taking a bit longer in the context of one-shot procedural generation `@tool` scripts.
- However, one thing that could easily mitigate this for the case of switching scenes is to simply run `OptimizeBroadPhase` when we find ourselves with no bodies left after running `JoltSpace3D::remove_object`, like what's shown in the code above. That should presumably be very quick, and would mean that switching scenes properly resets everything.
- The only problem with this is that there's this "default area" object (seen [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/e1b4101e3460dd9c6ba0b7f8d88e9751b8383f5b/modules/jolt_physics/jolt_physics_server_3d.cpp#L188-L192)) that always exists in every physics space (for questionable reasons) to represent things like default gravity and damping. This means we will never truly have 0 objects in any physics space, so we'll need to run `OptimizeBroadPhase` when we're down to 1 object instead, which starts to feel a bit hacky, but I guess that's fine.
- Bypassing (depending on how you look at it) the `!active` state (seen [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/e1b4101e3460dd9c6ba0b7f8d88e9751b8383f5b/modules/jolt_physics/jolt_physics_server_3d.cpp#L1617-L1619)) of the physics server and calling `JPH::PhysicsSystem::Update` with a delta of 0 on every editor physics tick would technically resolve both MRPs, along with their performance degradation, but only because the original MRP spreads out its operations across multiple physics frames, which I would argue is not really intuitive/typical for procedural generation `@tool` scripts. One-shot `@tool` scripts would still be able to run out of nodes, meaning we'd still need the above mentioned ability to query the broadphase for available nodes.

So the fixes would seem to be:

1. Using some ability to query `PhysicsSystem` for available space, run `OptimizeBroadPhase` in `JoltSpace3D::flush_pending_objects` when necessary, to prevent running out of nodes and crashing.
2. (Optionally) Run `OptimizeBroadPhase` in `JoltSpace3D::remove_object` when we're down to 1 object, to resolve any performance degradation from switching scenes.
3. (Optionally) Step `JPH::PhysicsSystem` with a delta of 0 on every editor physics tick, to resolve performance degradation more generally (but not completely).

I would be inclined to go with 1 and 2 but not 3. Perhaps this stance will age poorly, but I would prefer to see that `JoltPhysicsServer3D::step` remains a complete no-op when it's `!active`.

That's totally fine. I would be surprised if we get any more reports about this even after 4.5-stable is released, especially with #108239 merged. Either way, we'll include the eventual fix in the 4.5.1 patch. Absolute worst-case we just bring back the hacky `OptimizeBroadPhase` that #107454 removed and take the performance hit.

The fact that you're typically so readily available is not taken for granted either, of course.

I've written an implementation of `CanAddBodies`: https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/compare/master...feature/can_add_bodies, but I'm not very happy with it. It has to do several assumptions that may or may not hold:

* That the number of nodes used by a tree after maintenance is the size of the biggest of current/previous tree (actually it could be bigger if the splits end up differently than before).
* That the number of nodes needed to add nodes is a simple function of the number of bodies added (knowing how many you need means doing the actual work to add).

I haven't been able to come up with something that is guaranteed to overestimate the number of nodes needed. So it feels that this will just make it less likely that you run into issues instead of eliminating it.

As an alternative solution, I tried changing the signature of `BodyInterface::AddBodiesPrepare` so that it can return an error code when it runs out of nodes. The problem there is that `BodyInterface::AddBodiesFinalize` sometimes allocates a single node, so could fail in theory too. Also, on the next `PhysicsSystem::Update`, we build a new tree which could fail if all nodes were used up by the previous tree.

Finally, I have been thinking about providing some sort of health metric, but this also boils down to heuristics and I haven't been able to come up with something that feels like it's going to work.

Any ideas?

> The problem there is that `BodyInterface::AddBodiesFinalize` sometimes allocates a single node, so could fail in theory too. Also, on the next `PhysicsSystem::Update`, we build a new tree which could fail if all nodes were used up by the previous tree.

The `PhysicsSystem::Update` thing would seem to be a bit of a dealbreaker in this scenario, but is there any reason why `BodyInterface::AddBodiesFinalize` couldn't return an error code as well? I certainly wouldn't mind having a conditional `OptimizeBroadPhase` for both `AddBodiesPrepare` and `AddBodiesFinalize`.

Then again, we're calling one right after the other. Perhaps that makes less sense when using `AddBodiesPrepare` and `AddBodiesFinalize` for streaming purposes?

> but is there any reason why BodyInterface::AddBodiesFinalize couldn't return an error code as well?

Yes, that is indeed easy to fix. `PhysicsSystem::Update` is not however easily fixable (I don't see how in any case).

> `PhysicsSystem::Update` is not however easily fixable (I don't see how in any case).

What would you consider a fix in this case? Would it be feasible to have it return some new `EPhysicsUpdateError` as well, and the user could potentially do an `OptimizeBroadPhase` call and do the step again after that? If so, any reason why `PhysicsSystem::Update` couldn't do something similar internally without throwing the error?

> any reason why PhysicsSystem::Update couldn't do something similar internally without throwing the error?

The problem is that at all times there is a valid tree (because the tree is rebuilt while the physics sim is running and OptimizeBroadPhase can run concurrently with collision tests), so if you create a tree that eats up all nodes, then calling `OptimizeBroadPhase` doesn't have any nodes to create a new one. Nodes can be shared between trees, so we can also not split up the node pool into 2 pools. We need to somehow leave enough nodes for the new tree to be built.
